stages.title: Intermediate vocabulary
stages.hook: What is the difference between a "hobby", a "plan" and a "habit"? Intermediate words let you talk about your life.
explain: At the intermediate level you meet more abstract nouns: 約束 (yakusoku, promise or appointment), 経験 (keiken, experience), 準備 (junbi, preparation), 予定 (yotei, plan), 意見 (iken, opinion), 習慣 (shūkan, habit), 趣味 (shumi, hobby) and 大切 (taisetsu, important).

Many of these are two-kanji words from Chinese-derived (on) readings. Knowing the meaning of each kanji helps you guess new words: 準 (prepare) + 備 (equip) gives 準備. Verbs can be made from these nouns by adding する: 準備する (to prepare), 約束する (to promise).
Useful frames: 私の趣味は…です (my hobby is…), 予定があります (I have plans), 意見を言います (I give my opinion). Many kanji words are used in both Japanese and Chinese but sometimes with different meanings.
stages.mnemonic: Noun + する makes a verb: 準備する, 約束する.
sentences: I have no plans this weekend.

gq.q: How do you make "to prepare" from 準備?
gq.why: Adding する turns many nouns into verbs.

panel.q: What helps you guess a new two-kanji word?
panel.why: Knowing the meaning of each kanji helps you guess.

panel.q: A friend says 予定があります when invited. What might it mean?
panel.why: It means they have plans, often a polite way of declining.

panel.q: Why should learners be careful with kanji words shared with Chinese?
panel.why: Some words look the same but have different meanings.

teach.model: Nouns such as 趣味, 予定 and 習慣 let you talk about life. Adding する makes many nouns into verbs. Knowing each kanji helps you guess new words.

points.ask: How do I make a verb from a noun?

trip.prompt: Find five two-kanji words and break them into their parts.

stages.title: Verb forms and time expressions
stages.hook: How do you say "I ate", "I am eating" and "I have been to Japan"? Verb forms do the work.
explain: The dictionary form 食べる (taberu) is plain. The て-form 食べて (tabete) links actions and makes requests. The た-form 食べた (tabeta) is plain past, and the ない-form 食べない (tabenai) is plain negative. Polite forms are 食べます, 食べました and 食べません.

て-form + いる gives a progressive or resulting state: 今友達と話しています (I am talking with a friend now). た-form + ことがある says you have had an experience: 日本へ行ったことがあります (I have been to Japan). もう (already) and まだ (not yet) tell you how far an action has progressed.
Time expressions: さっき (a moment ago), これから (from now), いつも (always), ときどき (sometimes), よく (often). Japanese has only two tenses, past and non-past, so the non-past can also be the future: 明日行きます.
stages.mnemonic: て links; た is past; ない is not.
sentences: I am talking with a friend now.

gq.q: What does 日本へ行ったことがあります express?
o: I want to go to Japan
gq.why: た-form + ことがある expresses experience.

gq.q: Which form is the plain negative of 食べる?
gq.why: ない-form is the plain negative.

panel.q: How does Japanese show the future?
o: With the non-past form and time words
panel.why: Japanese has non-past and past, and the non-past also covers the future.

panel.q: What is the answer to もう食べましたか if you have not eaten?
panel.why: まだです means not yet.

panel.q: A learner says 今食べました to mean "I am eating now". What is the fix?
panel.why: The progressive uses て-form + います.

teach.model: The て-form links actions, the た-form is past and the ない-form is negative. て-form + いる gives a progressive, and た-form + ことがある gives experience. もう means already and まだ means not yet.

points.ask: What are もう and まだ?

trip.prompt: Make a table of the four forms for three verbs.

stages.title: Complex sentence introduction
stages.hook: How do you say "because it rained, I stayed home"? Connecting words build longer sentences.
explain: Japanese joins clauses with particles at the end of the first clause. から (kara) gives a reason: 雨が降ったから、家にいます (because it rained, I stay home). ので (node) is also because, and is softer and more polite. けど/けれど (keredo) means but, and のに (noni) means although, often with surprise.

たら (tara) means if or when: 時間があったら、行きます (if I have time, I will go). と (to) means whenever or if (natural results): 春になると、桜が咲きます (when spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom). ながら (nagara) joins two actions at once: 音楽を聞きながら勉強します.
In Japanese, the main verb or its ending comes last, and the clauses stack before it. ために (tame ni) shows a purpose: 日本語を勉強するために、日本へ行きます (to study Japanese, I go to Japan).
stages.mnemonic: The clause connector hides at the end of the first clause.
sentences: Because it rained, I am at home.
If I have time, I will go.
I study while listening to music.

gq.why: ので is a softer way to give a reason.
ながら joins actions done at once.

panel.q: Why is のに different from けど?
panel.why: のに expresses a contrast with surprise or complaint.

panel.q: A learner says 勉強するためにから. What is wrong?
panel.why: Two connectors are used together incorrectly.

panel.q: Which sentence uses と for a natural result?
o: 春になるから桜が咲きます
春になるのに桜が咲きます
春になると桜が咲きます
春になりながら咲きます
panel.why: と expresses a natural result in a general statement.

teach.model: Connectors like から, ので, けど, たら and ながら go at the end of the first clause. The main verb comes last. ので is softer than から.

points.ask: How do I give a reason?
Where does the main verb go?

trip.prompt: Find a list of conjunctive particles and write one sentence for each.

stages.title: Reading short stories
stages.hook: Many Japanese folk tales begin with "Long, long ago". What happens next in the story?
explain: Story words show the order of events. むかしむかし (mukashi mukashi) means long, long ago. ある日 (aru hi) means one day. すると (suruto) means then, そして (soshite) means and then, ところが (tokoro ga) means however or but then, やがて (yagate) means eventually and 最後に (saigo ni) means finally.
A typical tale: むかしむかし、おじいさんとおばあさんがいました。ある日、川で大きな桃を見つけました。 This is the opening of the folk tale Momotarō, the Peach Boy. Stories often end with めでたしめでたし (medetashi medetashi, and they lived happily).

When reading, the verb in plain form (です・ます or the plain style) tells the narrator's style. Folk tales often use plain past forms with だ・である. Skip unknown words, look for particles to find the subject, and check the endings for tense.
stages.mnemonic: Mukashi mukashi starts it, medetashi medetashi ends it.
sentences: Long ago there was an old man.
One day he found a big peach in the river.

gq.q: Which phrase begins a folk tale?
gq.why: むかしむかし means long, long ago.

gq.q: Which word signals a surprise or turn?
gq.why: ところが means but then.

panel.q: How do you find the subject in a long sentence?
o: Look for が or は
panel.why: Particles such as が and は show the subject or topic.

panel.q: What does めでたしめでたし suggest?
panel.why: It is a traditional ending meaning a happy end.

panel.q: Why do tales often use plain past forms?
panel.why: The narrative style uses plain forms instead of polite ones.

teach.model: Story words like むかしむかし, すると and 最後に show the order. Look for particles to find who does what, and check endings for tense.

points.ask: How do I find the subject?

trip.prompt: Read the summary of Momotarō and list its main events in order.

stages.title: Listening comprehension
stages.hook: Why does です sometimes sound like "dess"? Real Japanese speech shortens some vowels.
explain: In real Japanese, the vowels い and う are often almost silent between voiceless consonants. です (desu) sounds like "des", and ます (masu) like "mas". Listening practice means hearing both the written and the spoken forms.

Pitch accent matters: 橋 (hashi, bridge) and 箸 (hashi, chopsticks) are the same in kana but differ in pitch in the standard Tokyo pattern. Context usually makes the meaning clear. At stations, announcements such as 次は東京です (next is Tokyo) give key information in a fixed pattern.

Strategies: listen first for the topic (要点, yōten, the main point), catch numbers and place names, and ask for repeats: もう一度お願いします. Short signals (はい, ええ) from the listener are normal in conversation. Recording and replaying (録音) helps.
stages.mnemonic: Listen for the main point first.
sentences: Please speak a little more slowly.
I will note down the main points.
The next stop is Tokyo Station.

gq.q: How is です often pronounced in natural speech?
gq.why: The final vowel is often devoiced, sounding like "des".
要点 is the main point.

panel.q: What differs between 橋 and 箸?
panel.why: Standard Japanese distinguishes them by pitch accent.

panel.q: What is a good first step when listening to an announcement?
o: Listen for key place names and numbers
panel.why: Listen for the key information: place names and numbers.

panel.q: A learner cannot catch a phrase. What polite request helps?
o: もう一度お願いします
panel.why: もう一度お願いします asks for a repeat politely.

teach.model: Real speech shortens some vowels, so です sounds like "des". Pitch accent distinguishes words like hashi bridge and hashi chopsticks. Listen for the main point and key words first.

points.ask: What do I listen for first?

trip.prompt: Find an example of a pitch accent pair and listen to the audio.

stages.title: Conversation and pronunciation
stages.hook: The word ん is not like other kana: it can sound like n, m or ng. How do you pronounce Japanese clearly?
explain: Japanese has simple sounds, but timing matters. Each beat should be about equal. 長音 (chōon, long vowels) and 促音 (sokuon, doubled consonants) take extra beats: おばさん and おばあさん, きて and きって. 清音 (seion) are plain sounds, and 濁音 (dakuon) are voiced sounds such as が, ざ, だ and ば.

The Japanese r (ら行) is a light tap of the tongue, between English r, l and d. The ふ sound (fu) is made with both lips and no teeth. The sound ん (n) changes with the next sound: before p, b, m it sounds like m, as in さんぽ (sampo, a walk).

Intonation (抑揚, yokuyō) in Japanese is gentle. Questions are marked by か or rising intonation. Regional accent (方言, hōgen) varies, and the standard is based on the Tokyo speech of NHK-style broadcasts. Practise with shadowing: repeat just after a speaker.
stages.mnemonic: Equal beats, light r, changing ん.
sentences: I speak slowly in a loud voice.
I pay attention to the accent.

gq.q: How is the Japanese r usually made?
gq.why: It is a light tap of the tongue.

gq.q: What does a small っ do?
gq.why: A small っ doubles the next consonant with a beat of pause.

panel.q: How is ん in さんぽ pronounced?
panel.why: Before p, b and m, ん sounds like m.

panel.q: Why is "shadowing" useful?
panel.why: Repeating just after a speaker trains rhythm and pitch.

panel.q: A learner says おばさん for grandmother. What went wrong?
panel.why: The long vowel was shortened, giving "aunt".

teach.model: Keep beats equal, lengthen long vowels and double consonants properly, and use a light tap for r. ん changes with the next sound. Shadowing helps rhythm and pitch.

trip.prompt: Listen to a native speaker and shadow a short sentence.

stages.title: Writing paragraphs
stages.hook: Japanese writing paper has little squares. Where do you put the first character of a new paragraph?
explain: Traditional Japanese writing paper is 原稿用紙 (genkōyōshi), with a square for each character. A new paragraph (段落, danraku) begins with one empty square. Punctuation (句読点, kutōten) uses the comma 、 and the full stop 。, and quotation marks are 「 」.

Connecting words (接続詞, setsuzokushi) organise the text: まず (first), 次に (next), それから (after that), しかし (however) and 最後に (finally). In essays and reports, the plain style (だ・である) is often used, while letters and speeches use です・ます. Do not mix styles within a text.

A good paragraph has one main point, supporting details and a linking sentence. Check the particles は and が, the verb endings and the kanji. Use furigana or simple words if unsure, and read it aloud once.
stages.mnemonic: First まず, then 次に, after that それから, finally 最後に.

gq.q: Which mark is the Japanese full stop?

gq.why: まず means first of all.

panel.q: Why should you not mix the plain style and polite style in an essay?
panel.why: Mixing styles makes the text inconsistent.

panel.q: What does a new paragraph start with on genkōyōshi?
panel.why: One empty square is left at the start.

panel.q: Which connector shows contrast?
panel.why: しかし means however.

teach.model: A paragraph begins with one empty square. Use connectors such as まず, 次に and 最後に, and punctuation 、 and 。. Keep the style consistent, either plain or polite.

trip.prompt: Compare Japanese punctuation with English and list two differences.

stages.title: Cultural expressions and idioms
stages.hook: Why do Japanese speakers say "Let me disturb you" when entering a house? Some expressions come from custom.
explain: Many Japanese expressions reflect social habits. 頑張って (ganbatte) means do your best, and is said to someone before a test. お邪魔します (ojama shimasu, literally I will disturb you) is said when entering someone's home. お世話になります (osewa ni narimasu) expresses thanks for ongoing help.

The ideas of 本音 (honne, true feelings) and 建前 (tatemae, public stance) describe the difference between what is felt and what is said, to keep harmony. 空気を読む (kūki o yomu, to read the air) means to sense the mood. These are tendencies, not rules for every person.

Four-character idioms (四字熟語) from Chinese are also popular: 一期一会 (ichigo ichie) means one time, one meeting, treasure each meeting. 以心伝心 (ishin denshin) means heart-to-heart understanding without words. Idioms often cannot be translated word by word.
stages.mnemonic: Ganbatte for effort, ojama shimasu for entering.
items: thank you for your continuing help
sentences: Please do your best on the exam.
When I enter a house, I say ojama shimasu.
Reading the mood is also important.

gq.q: What do you say when entering a friend's home?
gq.why: お邪魔します is said on entering.
It means treasuring each meeting as a unique chance.

panel.q: What are honne and tatemae?
panel.why: They describe true feelings and public stance.

panel.q: Why is it unwise to say all Japanese people read the air?
o: They vary by person and context
panel.why: These are tendencies that vary by person and context.

panel.q: Which expression could you say to a friend before a match?
panel.why: 頑張って encourages effort.

teach.model: Expressions like ganbatte and ojama shimasu come from social habits. Honne and tatemae describe feelings and public stance. Four-character idioms such as ichigo ichie carry cultural ideas.

trip.prompt: Read about honne and tatemae and decide whether it is a rule or a tendency.

stages.title: Practical travel communication
stages.hook: You are at a station in Japan. How do you ask for a ticket and where the platform is?
explain: Travel words: 駅 (eki, station), 切符 (kippu, ticket), 電車 (densha, train), 新幹線 (Shinkansen, bullet train), ホテル (hoteru, hotel), パスポート (pasupōto, passport), 空港 (kūkō, airport) and 地図 (chizu, map).
To ask where something is, say すみません、駅はどこですか. To buy a ticket, say 東京までの切符を一枚ください (one ticket to Tokyo, please). Flat things such as tickets use the counter 枚 (mai). 〜まで means up to or until.

Etiquette: people queue at platforms, talk quietly on trains and avoid phone calls. IC cards such as Suica make fares simple. Many stations have English signs, but a few phrases help. Keep the passport for hotels, and say ありがとうございます to staff.
stages.mnemonic: すみません + place + どこですか gets you anywhere.
sentences: Excuse me, where is the station?

gq.q: Which counter is used for tickets?
gq.why: 枚 is the counter for flat things like tickets.
まで means up to or until.

panel.q: Which is the polite way to ask for directions?
o: すみません、駅はどこですか
panel.why: すみません starts politely.

panel.q: Why are tickets counted with 枚 and not 人?
o: Counters depend on the kind of object
panel.why: Counters depend on the kind of thing counted: 枚 for flat things, 人 for people.

panel.q: At a hotel desk, which item would you need to show?
panel.why: Hotels in Japan commonly ask foreign guests for their passport.

teach.model: To ask where a place is, say すみません and the place は どこですか. To buy a ticket, say the destination まで の 切符 を 一枚 ください. Tickets are counted with 枚.

points.ask: How do I ask where something is?
How do I ask for a ticket?
What counter do I use for tickets?

trip.prompt: Find how the Shinkansen began and note the year it opened.
